key_terms.meaning: Anything access is controlled on: a file, a memory page, a printer, a device, a socket.
Permission to perform one named operation on an object, such as read, write or execute.
The system checks every single access at the moment it happens, instead of trusting the program to behave.
Every process holds only the rights its current job needs, and no more.
When no rule grants access, the answer is deny.
The rules (who may do what) are kept separate from the code that enforces them, so rules can change without rewriting the kernel.
The set of rights a process holds at a given moment; rights = pairs of (object, operations allowed).
An entry point that checks the caller's rights before it runs; a process can change domain only through such a point.
Running a program whose set-user-ID bit is on, so the process takes on the file owner's user id and that owner's domain.
A table with domains as rows and objects as columns; entry (i, j) is the set of rights domain i has on object j.
One column of the access matrix stored with the object: a list of (domain, rights) for that object.
One row of the access matrix stored with the domain: a list of (object, rights) that the domain holds.
Taking back a right that was granted earlier, which is hard because copies of the right may sit in other domains.
An unforgeable ticket that names an object and carries the rights to it, so holding the ticket is the proof of permission.
Proving a claimed identity before any rights are looked up.
A log of security-relevant events, kept so an attack can be detected and reconstructed afterwards.
A counter that numbers events so that if event a happens before event b, then C(a) < C(b); it measures order, not seconds.
The rule that decides whether a client's cached copy or the server's copy is current, and what to do when they differ.
Linux keeps nine permission bits per file (read, write, execute for owner, group, others) plus three special bits.
A numeric name for a Windows user or group; access lists are written in SIDs, not in login names.

takeaways: Protection is inside the computer and checks each access; security is about deliberate attackers outside and inside.
A domain is just the current list of (object, rights) a process holds, and every domain change must pass through a guarded point.
The whole protection state fits into one access matrix, and real systems store it by columns (access lists) or by rows (capabilities).
Revocation is easy for access lists and hard for capabilities, because a capability can be copied without the object knowing.
Least privilege and fail-safe defaults prevent most damage even when a program is buggy.
Every defence is only as strong as the weakest of authentication, authorisation, isolation and audit.
A distributed system has no shared memory and no global clock, so processes must order events with logical clocks instead of wall time.
Caching is what makes a distributed file system fast, and also what makes it inconsistent.
Linux mode bits are a short access list per file; Windows stores a full access list of SIDs, which allows far finer sharing.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit usually expect a drawn access matrix, a clear access-lists-versus-capabilities comparison, and then the same ideas applied to Linux and Windows in the case-study question.

bank.q: Define protection and security. State the goals of protection and explain least privilege, fail-safe defaults and separation of policy from mechanism with one example each.
outline: Protection: internal mechanism that checks whether a subject may use an object in the requested way
Security: defence against deliberate attack from outside or inside
Goals: controlled access, prevention of misuse of rights, detection of programming errors
Least privilege: give only the rights needed now
Fail-safe defaults: deny when no rule grants
Policy versus mechanism: rules stored as data, kernel only enforces

bank.q: Explain the access matrix model. How is it implemented by access lists and by capability lists? Give one advantage and one disadvantage of each.
outline: Rows = domains, columns = objects, cell = set of rights
Access list: column stored with the object; easy to see who can use a file, hard to answer what a process can use
Capability list: row stored with the domain; fast check at use time, hard to revoke
Access list used by Linux and Windows; capability list used in tagged architectures and in capability OS designs
Sparse matrix in practice, so neither form stores all cells

bank.q: What is a protection domain? Explain how a process changes domain, using setuid execution and a guarded procedure.
outline: Domain = current set of rights of a process
Rights are (object, operations) pairs
Domain change only through controlled entry points
setuid exec: file owner's id becomes process user id, so domain changes to the owner's
sudo: a guarded program that checks the user against a configuration file and then runs the command in the root domain
Danger: a bug inside a privileged domain is a security hole

bank.q: What is revocation of access rights? Why is it difficult? Explain reacquisition, back-pointers and indirection as ways of making it work.
outline: Revocation = withdrawing a right already granted
Difficult because copies of a capability may exist in many processes
Reacquisition: re-ask for rights periodically
Back-pointers: object keeps a list of who holds a capability, so copies can be found
Indirection: capabilities point to a table entry, deleting the entry kills all copies at once
Access lists make revocation trivial: edit the list

bank.q: A system has three domains D1, D2, D3 and three objects File1, File2, Printer. D1 holds read on File1 and write on File2; D2 holds execute on File1; D3 holds write on Printer and read on File2. Draw the access matrix and write out the access lists and the capability lists.
outline: Matrix of 3 rows and 3 columns with empty cells left blank
Access list for each object: list the (domain, rights) entries
Capability list for each domain: list the (object, rights) entries
Point out that each form contains exactly the same non-empty cells
Note the size difference when the matrix is sparse

bank.q: Using a capability machine, show how a print server can accept jobs from a program without giving that program any other right. Explain what stops the program from forging a capability for another device.
outline: Capability = object identifier plus rights, held in a protected area the program cannot read or write
Printer capability carries only the write-job right
Forgery prevented by tagging memory words as capability or data and by hardware checks on capability registers
Kernel creates and destroys capabilities; user code can only copy or pass them through controlled calls
Compare with access lists, where the print server checks an identity at each request

bank.q: Three processes P1, P2, P3 exchange messages. P1 does a then sends m1 to P2; P2 receives m1 then does b; P3 does c then sends m2 to P2, and P2 receives m2 after b. Assign Lamport timestamps and state the resulting order of events.
outline: Rule: each event increments the local counter; receipt sets counter to max(local, received) + 1
a before send m1; received timestamp carried in the message
b and c are concurrent: neither happens before the other
Total order obtained by breaking ties with process id
Show the final sequence of (event, counter, process)

bank.q: A distributed file system lets clients cache file blocks. For a sequence where client A reads a block, client B writes it, and A reads again, explain what A may return under write-through and write-back caching, and how a lease would fix it.
outline: With write-through, server copy is fresh but A's cache may be stale
With write-back, B's write may not have reached the server at all
Staleness window and its length
Callbacks or leases: the server promises to recall a cached copy before allowing a conflicting write
Consistency versus availability trade-off

bank.q: A Linux file has mode 754. The owner is ravi, the group is project, and the file is a program. State who can read, write and execute it, and what happens when a user outside the group runs it.
outline: 7 = rwx for owner, 5 = r-x for group, 4 = r-- for others
Owner ravi: read, write, execute; group members: read and execute; others: read only
A user outside the group gets the others class, so the execute bit is off and the kernel returns permission denied
Show that permissions are checked at open/exec time against the process's user and group ids
Mention that a directory needs the x bit to be entered

bank.q: Compare Linux mode bits with Windows access lists. Why does a general-purpose server need access lists, and what does an access list cost that mode bits do not?
outline: Mode bits: one owner, one group, one others class, three rights, stored in the inode
Windows: each object has a discretionary access list of (SID, access mask) entries, with allow and deny entries
Need: many users, many groups, different rights per user, inheritance from folders
Cost: longer check per open, more storage, more complex administration
Both are access-list implementations of the access matrix column

bank.q: Explain program threats: Trojan horse, trap door, logic bomb, stack and buffer overflow, and virus. For each, name one defence and say what property of the defence limits it.
outline: Trojan horse: hidden harmful code inside a useful program; signed packages limit it, but trust in the signer remains
Trap door: secret entry left by the author; code review and rebuilds limit it
Logic bomb: code that triggers on a condition; hard to detect statically
Buffer overflow: writing past an array overflows the return address; bounds checks, non-executable stack, address randomisation
Virus: code that copies itself into other programs; antivirus signatures fail against new variants
General point: isolation and least privilege limit the damage, audit detects it

bank.q: A distributed system has no global clock. Evaluate the consequences for mutual exclusion and for file caching, and judge when physical time synchronisation is an acceptable substitute for logical clocks.
outline: No shared memory, so all coordination is by messages
No global clock, so we cannot say which of two events happened first by time stamp alone
Lamport happens-before ordering and vector clocks give causal order
Distributed mutual exclusion built on logical clocks or on a token
File caching with leases needs an agreed notion of lease expiry
Physical time via NTP is acceptable when clocks stay within a known bound and the cost of an occasional wrong ordering is small

bank.q: 'sudo and setuid programs are the biggest holes in an otherwise least-privilege system.' Evaluate this claim and suggest controls that reduce the risk.
outline: Least privilege says run with only the needed rights; a privileged program is a deliberate exception
Any bug in a setuid-root program runs with root rights, so it can be exploited
sudo restricts who may become root and logs it, but a misconfigured rule is equally dangerous
Controls: keep privileged programs small, audit them, drop privileges after the privileged step, log every use, prefer fine-grained capabilities over full root
Trade-off: usability versus blast radius

glossary.def: The internal mechanism that decides, for each access, whether a subject may use an object in the way requested.
Defence of the system and its data against deliberate attack, whether from outside or from an authorised user.
The active party asking for access, normally a process acting for a user.
One permitted operation on one object, for example read on a file.
Moving a process from one set of rights to another, allowed only through a controlled entry point.
Give each process only the rights its present task needs.
Require more than one condition, or more than one party, before a sensitive operation is allowed.
Keep the protection code small and simple, because every extra line is a possible hole.
A table of domains against objects whose cells hold the permitted rights.
The list of domains and their rights stored with a single object.
A protected token naming an object together with rights to it, unforgeable by user code.
A hardware register whose contents the running program cannot modify, used to hold a capability.
The small part of a system that must be correct for protection to hold.
Withdrawal of a right after it was granted, including every copy of it.
Proving that a subject is who it claims to be.
Deciding what an authenticated subject is allowed to do.
Recording security-relevant events so an attack can be detected and traced.
Writing past the end of an array and overwriting nearby memory, often the return address.
A hidden entry point left in a program that skips the normal checks.
A set of independent computers that appear to users as one system and cooperate by passing messages.
Event a happens before event b if a could have influenced b through program order or message passing.
A counter value assigned to each event so that happens-before implies a smaller timestamp.
A file system whose files are stored on several servers but shown to clients as one set of files.
The property that a client never acts on a cached copy that is out of date beyond the agreed rules.
